Designer and builder in Norwalk, Connecticut — making things that make sense of a place.

I'm Ed. I run a small design studio that now makes games, publish a daily civic brief for my city, keep a sourced ledger of surveillance-tech failures, DJ weddings, and build private tools for my family and myself.
“What I build when nobody asked me to.”
Off the clock: wedding dance floors since 2000, and more city meeting agendas than anyone should read.
Four games out of ET3 Media: a song toy, two text games set in 1986, and an off-road driver built for a club.

An '80s step-sequencer toy. Tap a glowing grid and hear a song: up to sixteen bars of lo-fi, '80s hip hop or EDM, every sound synthesized. Then pass the jam — friends add two bars a turn until the song is done.
Free to play, with one Sound Pack to unlock the rest. A shared song opens in the browser, no app needed.

A retro text horror game for phones. Seven nights as the new counselor at Camp Moonwick in 1986: three choices per event, four meters — nerve, trust, cheer and battery — 181 events and 43 endings, 33 of them deaths.
The free game is all seven nights, with a real way to survive them.
A retro time-loop text game. It's prom night, 1986, from eight o'clock to midnight — again, and again. Keep your cool and your nerve, and carry what each loop teaches you into the next.
Same studio kit as Pixel Jam, and its music is a cousin of Pixel Jam's menu tune.
Client game · Northeast Land Rover Club

A 3D off-road game ET3 Media is building for the Northeast Land Rover Club, at NELRC.ai: the club's trucks on six trails — rocks, mud, sand, water crossings and snow, a winch when you need one, and the crew on the radio when you don't make it.
Built for a club, played in the browser. Proof the studio builds games for other people too.
※ The private projects are described, never linked — on purpose.

A daily civic brief for Norwalk, Connecticut. It reads the city's meeting agendas, packets and minutes, local news, public filings, weather and tides, and publishes before breakfast — with a Sunday newsletter and a full Spanish edition.

The public record is public but scattered across portals nobody has time to read. The Sound puts it in one place. Anything interpretive is AI-drafted and held for human review; the record itself is published verbatim; no names from police logs, ever.

A running, sourced timeline of how license-plate readers, body cameras, AI report-writers and the rest of the "public-safety technology" market are actually going — and what the failures cost taxpayers. THE TAB, in the corner, adds up the documented public money.

The format is borrowed, with credit, from Web3 Is Going Just Great. Nothing publishes until code has confirmed a fetched source supports the claim, the date and the dollar figure. The entries are deadpan; the facts carry the irony.

My design studio. Custom websites, brand identities, print and signage for small businesses in Connecticut and beyond, games for phones and the web — plus the automation that keeps a one-person studio running.
It is also the publisher behind The Norwalk Sound and Nothing To See Here. If you need something built, this is the door.

My DJ side hustle. ChewyDown Productions has played weddings and private events since 2000, mainly in the Hudson Valley and across the tri-state area, alongside my best friend from childhood, DJ Big Mike.
The oldest project here by a couple of decades, and the only one whose success is measured by a full dance floor.
A private archive for two families: a tree, people pages, recipes, photos and stories, built to one standard — could your grandmother use it on her phone, alone, on the first try?

A news-intelligence briefing built for one reader. It clusters the same healthcare story across outlets and writes a daily brief under one rule: never state a fact that wasn't in the headline or the blurb.
※ No link: single-reader tool behind a login.

Two browser-only tools for a college marketing team: campaign CSVs into charts and branded PDFs, and ad copy tested against fifteen synthetic student personas before it runs. No install, no server; the data never leaves the machine.
※ No link: lives on an internal network drive.
